blocks.text: Billy laid the morning newspaper beside his notebook and smoothed the fold.
blocks.alt: Billy sorts newspaper clippings about the stolen ray and missing tank, building and vault at the operations desk.

blocks.text: The bank story occupied half a page.
A guard had found the delivery doors open. Inside the renovation annex, the vault was gone. The photograph showed a broad, empty patch of floor where the steel strongroom had stood.
Billy read the account twice.
No smashed walls. No wreckage dragged through the doorway. No explanation for how something so heavy had left the building.
He took the scissors from the desk drawer.
On the corkboard behind him, two older cuttings waited beneath red drawing pins.
ARMY RAY STOLEN.
TANK MISSING.
He had kept them after the demonstration. The Army wanted its experimental device back. It wanted the tank back too. Witnesses had seen the tank disappear from the display before the thief escaped.
Billy turned to the pile beside the telephone and found another cutting.
BUILDING VANISHES.
The address was familiar. Daniel Orkleson’s old laboratory had stood there.

Billy had copied the address into his notebook when the report first appeared. The photograph showed the neighboring buildings and the space between them. The laboratory itself had vanished. Nobody had seen a demolition crew. Nobody had seen it leave.
He put the two photographs side by side.
Billy drew the desk lamp closer.
The Army article described the demonstration. Equipment had been reduced for transport, then restored to its original size.
He underlined the last part.
Restored.
He looked back at the missing laboratory’s address.
The police had taken evidence from the old workshop. Orkleson had escaped. Flaming Head’s later account, passed on by Seth, placed him at another machine with Laura beside him.
Billy opened those notes.
The collector had been wrecked. Orkleson had still been there when Flaming Head left.
He turned back to the newspaper photograph.
The vanished laboratory might still be standing somewhere else.
Billy slid off the chair and carried the cuttings to the board.
He pinned the missing building beneath the stolen ray. The vault went beside it, under the tank.
From the drawer he took a spool of red thread.
The first strand joined the ray to the tank. They had disappeared at the same demonstration.
Another joined the ray to the building.
He paused before tying the next one. Then he read the bank account again and ran a strand to the vault.
One machine. Three disappearances.
That did not prove who had used it.
He wrote ORKLESON on a card and added a question mark. Then he moved the threads around the card so he could follow every connection without taking the papers down.
blocks.alt: Billy connects four newspaper stories with red thread around a card marked Orkleson on his corkboard.

blocks.text: Billy stood back.

He telephoned the police and gave the dates and addresses from his notebook. He asked whether the Army’s account mentioned an older man with enormous round spectacles or a floating head with metal teeth.
blocks.alt: Billy reaches for the corded telephone beside his completed newspaper board, ready to follow the connection.

blocks.text: While he waited for the answer, he opened the street atlas.
The old laboratory’s location was already marked. He put a small square around the bank.
They told him someone would check the demonstration report. Billy wrote down the name, thanked them and put the receiver back.
He had no new address for Orkleson. He had a building to look for.
He pulled a fresh sheet toward him and began listing the industrial streets where an unfamiliar laboratory might stand among workshops and warehouses.
Behind him, the scanner crackled.
Billy listened, pencil held above the paper. An ordinary traffic call. He returned to the map.
His eyes went once more to the board.
The vault meant money. The missing laboratory gave Orkleson somewhere to work.
And he had a tank.
Billy set the pencil down.
Orkleson was planning something big.
